stem: A genomics company just created a new S3 general purpose bucket and wants to keep using SSE-C there for a legacy pipeline that supplies its own encryption keys, while a separate team wants to cut the AWS KMS request costs on a different, SSE-KMS-encrypted bucket that receives millions of PUT requests a day. Which TWO actions address these two goals? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Assume SSE-C already works on the new bucket, since it always has in the past
Explicitly re-enable SSE-C on the new bucket through its PutBucketEncryption configuration
Enable an S3 Bucket Key on the high-volume SSE-KMS bucket
Switch the high-volume bucket from SSE-KMS to DSSE-KMS to reduce its AWS KMS request costs
Disable default encryption entirely on the new bucket so SSE-C requests are no longer blocked

rationale: Since April 2026, S3 automatically disables SSE-C on new general purpose buckets, so the pipeline needs an explicit PutBucketEncryption configuration re-enabling it before SSE-C uploads will succeed. An S3 Bucket Key reuses a short-lived, bucket-level data key instead of calling AWS KMS on every request, cutting the KMS request costs on the high-volume bucket by up to 99%. Assuming SSE-C still works by default is exactly the assumption the April 2026 change breaks, since new buckets now reject SSE-C uploads until it is re-enabled. DSSE-KMS costs more than SSE-KMS because it performs additional KMS operations for its second encryption layer, which moves the high-volume bucket's costs in the wrong direction. Disabling default encryption controls a different setting entirely; it does not re-enable SSE-C and would leave uploads without any server-side encryption configured by default.
